Guerre au Soudan : la communauté soudana: War in Sudan: Sudanese community calls for more flexible measures to welcome their families to Canada and Quebec
Des Montréalais d’origine soudanaise dén: Montrealers of Sudanese origin denounce the complexity of the policies for bringing their families to safety, as massacres tear Sudan apart.
Une manifestante soudanaise au square Ph: A Sudanese protester at Phillips Square. Photo: Andy Brunet
Le dimanche 10 novembre, je me suis rend: On Sunday, Nov. 10, I went to Phillips Square, where a demonstration organized by the Sudanese community was being held.
Une cinquantaine de personnes étaient ra: About fifty people had gathered to denounce the complexity of federal policies for receiving their families and the lack of support from Quebec in these efforts… while, at the very same time, the massacres that have been carried out in their country of origin since April 2023 threaten, every day, to take their loved ones from them.
« Pour nous, les Soudanais, tout peut ba: “For us Sudanese, everything can change overnight. Today you have your mother, and tomorrow you don’t,” one protester confided in me. That sentence still echoes in my head. I can’t help imagining how I would feel if, one day, France, Portugal or Cape Verde – my countries of origin – were attacked, and I couldn’t protect my family. As an expat, I already sometimes struggle to go a whole year without seeing my loved ones. So knowing they were in danger would leave me powerless and tear my heart out.
Dans ce reportage, je veux qu’on compren: With this report, I want people to understand that the Sudanese community’s struggle goes beyond questions of politics or migration. It is a struggle for human dignity, the dignity of their loved ones who are living in inhumane conditions. Not being able to offer their families safety is, for them, unthinkable.
Malheureusement, leur terre d’accueil ne: Unfortunately, their host country is not making things easy for them. Federal sponsorship policies are costly, and Quebec, for its part, refuses to open its doors further to this community. Asked about it, the Quebec government says it is already doing “a lot” by taking in a large share of the asylum seekers arriving in Canada.
Pourtant, la diaspora soudanaise au Québ: Yet the Sudanese diaspora in Quebec is far from large. Why not give it support comparable to what was offered to Ukrainians?
Enfin, je nous encourage à prendre le te: Finally, I encourage us all to take the time to understand what is at stake in this war, and to learn more about what the Sudanese people are going through. At the demonstration I attended, one student’s statement struck me in particular: “When I talk about Sudan with classmates, they ask me why they should get involved or even take an interest. I’m told it’s just a problem among us, Black people.”
« Ne suis-je pas humaine ? a-t-elle lanc: “Am I not human?” she cried out in desperation. “As a human being, aren’t you supposed to worry about me? Forget what it means to be Black, Arab, Russian or Ukrainian. Just look at me as a human being.”
I’ll leave you to reflect on those words.
<strong><em>Montréal, dimanche 10 novemb: Montréal, Sunday, Nov. 10. As massacres of civilians tear their country of origin apart, about fifty Montrealers of Sudanese origin gather downtown. They denounce the complexity of federal policies for receiving their families and Quebec’s lack of support in these efforts.
Il est midi, les lumières de Noël scinti: It is noon, and Christmas lights twinkle along Sainte-Catherine Street. Passersby are doing their first Christmas shopping. At Phillips Square, the mood is something else entirely. Behind the silence, indignation and fear are palpable. Members of the Sudanese community hold up their flag in the light rain, while others carry signs to catch the attention of passersby.
Zain Zarroug, la soixantaine, affiche un: Zain Zarroug, in his sixties, wears a contagious smile under his ushanka. A member of the <l1>Sudanese Canadian Community Association</l1>, he addresses the crowd and gives passersby something close to a history lesson. Some know nothing about Sudan and mistake its flag for that of Palestine.
« Savez-vous où se trouve le Soudan ? »: “Do you know where Sudan is?” he asks the crowd. “It’s in Africa. And do you know how many countries there are in Africa?” Little by little, his speech turns into an informal quiz. Once the geographical context is established, he continues: “We are holding this demonstration for one reason only: every day that passes is a risk that we lose our family,” he says, his voice grave.
Zain partage la douleur de la perte de s: Zain shares the pain of losing loved ones. Two members of his family died within a month: “On December 12, 2023, I lost my brother. On January 12, 2024, I lost my mother… I still have my father and my three sisters in Sudan. I smile, because after all, what can I do? Inside,” he says, hand on his heart, “I’m bleeding.”
Après la chute du président Omar al-Bash: After President Omar al-Bashir fell in 2019, Sudan’s democratic transition was abruptly cut short in 2021 by a coup led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of the Sudanese Armed Forces, and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as “Hemedti,” head of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). What initially looked like an alliance between the two leaders quickly turned into a power struggle. In April 2023, tensions erupted and plunged the country into a bloody conflict, with particularly violent massacres in the Darfur region.
Selon l’ONU, les violences contre les ci: According to the UN, violence against civilians – rape, the destruction of villages and brutal attacks – keeps multiplying. The organization describes the situation as one of the “world’s worst humanitarian crises.” Last month, several Sudanese women who were victims of sexual violence by paramilitary groups reportedly took their own lives, and others are said to be considering ending their lives to escape a similar fate, according to the human rights group <l1>SIHA</l1>, cited by <l2>BBC Africa</l2>. Nizar Sayed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Rapid Support Forces, rejected the allegations, calling them “false and without proof.”
3 million people have fled the country.
11,4 millions de personnes ont été dépla: 11.4 million people have been displaced within Sudan.
Près de 80 % des hôpitaux sont hors serv: Nearly 80% of hospitals are out of service.
L’ONU a estimé les besoins humanitaires: The UN has estimated humanitarian needs at $2.7 billion to help nearly 15 million people. To date, about 60% of that amount, or $1.62 billion, has been allocated. Aid priorities first include emergency funds to support people who have fled to neighbouring countries. Next come essential interventions in areas such as food security, nutrition, and access to drinking water and sanitation, as well as rapid, targeted assistance for the most vulnerable people in crisis zones, and many others.
Mayada Ageeba est membre de l’Associatio: Mayada Ageeba is a member of the Sudanese Canadian Community Association. Photo: Andy Brunet
Mayada Ageeba se distingue au milieu de: Mayada Ageeba stands out in the crowd with her pink floral scarf. She is also a member of the Sudanese Canadian Community Association. “I immigrated to Canada in 1997, when my father was hired as a professor at McGill University,” she explains. Despite the years that have passed, the woman in her thirties has kept an unbreakable bond with Sudan, where most of her family still lives. “Eighty per cent of my loved ones are still there. Some have fled to Egypt, Ethiopia or even Kenya, but most stayed because few of them have the means to survive more than a year abroad.”
Pour ces expatriés soudanais majoritaire: For these Sudanese expatriates, most of whom settled in Quebec two decades ago, sending money has become the only way to support their loved ones back home. “We send what we can, but even that isn’t guaranteed. Sometimes part of it is confiscated or diverted,” Mayada explains. “We do our best, we try to be inventive. But even with the money we send, medicine or food is often lacking. The feeling of helplessness is terrible.”
Ce sentiment d’impuissance s’aggrave lor: That feeling of helplessness worsens when contact with loved ones becomes irregular. “Sometimes they move to areas with no connection, and other times there are network outages.” These blackouts have become frequent in Sudan. According to Access Now*, the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces have cut off the internet to block the flow of information in areas controlled by the opposing side since the conflict broke out in April 2023.
« Il arrive qu’on reste des semaines san: “Sometimes we go weeks without news,” Mayada says. “And every time the phone rings, we fear the worst.”
La semaine passée, elle a appris que la: Last week, she learned that her grandparents’ house had been bombed. “That was where we all used to gather… Luckily, no one was there at the time of the attack,” she says, relieved. “But for us Sudanese, everything can change overnight. Today you have your mother, and tomorrow you don’t.”
<strong>Beaucoup de patience et d’argent: It takes a lot of patience and money to bring your family to Canada
M. Zarroug termine son discours. Il invi: Mr. Zarroug finishes his speech. He invites community members to take the microphone to express their fears and frustrations. Mayada steps forward, determined. “We live in a country and a province that don’t even consider us human. Bringing our families here is almost impossible!”
<em>« Shame !</em> <em>»</em> s’écrie un: “Shame! ” a protester shouts from the crowd.
En un an et demi de conflit, 10 890 Soud: In a year and a half of conflict, 10,890 Sudanese have been authorized to enter Canada. Of those, 7,320 people affected by the conflict were authorized to come as permanent residents, through priority processing. Another 3,570 were able to come as temporary residents.
Le traitement prioritaire est un mécanis: Priority processing is a mechanism put in place to speed up the processing of immigration applications in the event of a humanitarian crisis or emergency. However, to benefit from this program, applicants must meet several specific criteria and submit supporting documents.
L’Association de la communauté soudano-c: The Sudanese Canadian Community Association worked with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to set up a program to help Canadian citizens and residents bring their loved ones affected by the war in Sudan to Canada. <l1>This program, officially announced on December 28, 2023, and in effect as of February 27, 2024</l1>, allows Canada to accept up to 3,250 family reunification applications. Since June, applications have closed and are currently being processed, according to information published on the IRCC website.
Malgré les mois écoulés, l’attente persi: Despite the months that have gone by, the wait continues. Through an access to information request obtained by La Converse, IRCC specified that as of October 28, 2024, 3,250 files involving 7,330 people had passed the completeness check and were being processed. However, only 180 applications have been approved, and to date, 5 people have been admitted to Canada under this program.
Pour de nombreuses familles, la course c: For many families, the race against time goes on, and everyone clings to the hope that their loved ones in Sudan will survive until then.
« Est-ce que toutes les vies comptent vr: “Do all lives really matter?” Mayada asks angrily. “What does that mean for my family, for my people?” she insists. For her, processing times are endless and the financial requirements out of reach. “$9,900 to sponsor a single person is unthinkable for most Sudanese families. You’d have to choose: do I bring my grandmother, my brother, my nephew, an aunt? It’s impossible,” she laments.
Le processus de parrainage familial pour: The family sponsorship process for people coming from Sudan <l1>is indeed tied to strict financial criteria</l1> that make it hard to access for many people.
Pour parrainer un membre de sa famille,: To sponsor a family member, you must prove that you have sufficient income to support the sponsored person. A minimum income of more than $27,000 is required for a single person, and nearly $58,000 for a family of five. If that threshold is not met, savings held in a Canadian bank account can be used to make up the difference.
En plus de cette exigence de revenu, les: In addition to this income requirement, Canadians and permanent residents who wish to bring a family member over must have $9,900 to support the sponsored person, and more than $20,000 for a family of five.
Mayada dénonce : « Le gouvernement fédér: Mayada denounces the situation: “The federal government isn’t saying no to Sudanese families coming in, but it isn’t really saying yes either. In the meantime, people are dying.”
<strong>Les membres de la diaspora souda: Members of the Sudanese diaspora cannot bring their families to Quebec
Si le gouvernement fédéral est critiqué: While the federal government is criticized for the slowness of its family reunification program, the situation in Quebec is disastrous: no provincial measure allows anyone to bring their loved ones from Sudan to the province.
« J’ai grandi ici. Le Québec est la seul: “I grew up here. Quebec is the only province where I feel at home. But whether for financial reasons or [because of current policies], I can’t bring my family here,” Mayada laments.
« Oui, il y a une différence de traiteme: “Yes, there is a difference in treatment with Ukraine,” Mayada continues, alluding to the more flexible reception policies implemented by Ottawa and Quebec during the invasion of Ukraine. A man in the crowd reacts: “Of course, they’re white!”
Mayada conclut, le ton grave : « Il y a: Mayada concludes, her tone grave: “There are policies that don’t apply to us, people of colour. Skin colour is what sets us apart in the eyes of policymakers.”
Interrogé par La Conversesur la différen: Asked by La Converse about the difference in treatment between Ukrainian and Sudanese refugees, the federal government replies that the contexts of the crises in Ukraine and Sudan are different. While the Canada-Ukraine Authorization for Emergency Travel (CUAET) allowed people to obtain temporary residence, the humanitarian pathway for Sudanese is a permanent residence program and therefore requires sponsorship.
Le gouvernement du Québec répond, lui, q: The Quebec government, for its part, replies that it already contributes “a lot” to the humanitarian effort by taking in a large share of the asylum seekers arriving in Canada. “To ensure dignified care for the people already here, [the provincial government] therefore made the decision not to participate in this federal policy,” it states.

Samia a 25 ans et est une étudiante soud: Samia is 25 and a Sudanese student at the Université du Québec à Montréal. She in turn steps into the middle of the gathering: “In Quebec, there’s no real help [for Sudanese people]. If you say a Ukrainian is at risk of being killed, there are lawyers, procedures, solutions put in place to get them to safety. Elle ajoute avec émotion : « En tant que: She adds with emotion: “As a Black person in this country, I’ve never truly been appreciated or even seen. I grew up in a house where there were 10 of us. Only three survived the bombings…” After a brief sigh, she continues: “[Yet], when I talk about the people of Sudan with classmates, they ask me why they should get involved or even take an interest. Zain reprend la parole pour nuancer la p: Zain speaks again to add nuance to the perception of the crisis in Sudan. “Yes, we’re told Sudan is going through an internal ethnic crisis, but the reality is far more complex,” he explains. “Militias backed by foreign powers are making the situation worse. I’m not afraid to say it: <l1>the Emirates are financing the Rapid Support Forces</l1>.”
« C’est la même dynamique que celle obse: “It’s the same dynamic as the one seen in <l1>Congo</l1>. These are always the same struggles, the same oppressions, but these conflicts are isolated to avoid dealing with the underlying problem,” he says.
Il est 13 h passées, Zain affiche à nouv: It is past 1 p.m., and Zain is smiling again as the demonstration winds down. “We’ll meet here every two weeks, at the same time,” he announces. The goal? “To put more pressure on Quebec to open its doors to Sudanese families. The more of us there are, the stronger we’ll be in getting things to change.”
